opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I was thinking about what to work on during my PhD, I noticed that the frontier of model training had shifted heavily toward industry. Pretraining a large model takes thousands of GPUs and a huge engineering team, and an academic lab simply can't compete there. If you try, you're always a step behind, and your results get overtaken by whatever the big companies release next month.

Systems felt different. Once these models exist, someone has to make them run efficiently. Inference, serving, memory management, scheduling, compilation: these problems don't need a ten-thousand-GPU cluster to study. You can make real progress with a handful of GPUs and a good idea. And the impact is very direct. If you make inference twice as fast, everyone who deploys a model benefits right away.

There's also a nice property: systems work compounds through open source. A paper might be read by a few hundred people. A well-maintained open-source system can be used by thousands of companies and researchers, and their feedback tells you which problems actually matter. For an academic lab, that's a way to have industry-scale influence without industry-scale resources. You become part of the infrastructure that everyone builds on.

Finally, I just enjoyed it. Machine-learning systems sit at the intersection of understanding the models and understanding the hardware. You need to know why attention behaves a certain way, and also how GPU memory works and how a compiler turns your Python into kernels. I found that combination intellectually satisfying, and I felt it was a space where a student could carve out a real niche and grow alongside the field.

r001.rationale: The response says systems research can make progress with a handful of GPUs and spread through open source to thousands of companies and researchers, giving an academic lab industry-scale influence without industry-scale resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it came from a feeling of frustration during my PhD. I was working on transfer learning and domain adaptation at Tsinghua, and I kept noticing that a lot of the "research" in that space was about squeezing out another half a percent on a benchmark. You write a paper, you get it accepted, and then nobody uses the method. That felt hollow to me.

Around the same time, I started noticing that the real bottleneck for a lot of people was not the algorithm, it was the system. People had ideas they could not test because training was too slow, or memory ran out, or the framework did something weird under the hood that nobody understood. I remember spending days just figuring out why a model was slow, and realizing that almost nobody in an academic lab actually understood the whole stack from Python down to the GPU kernel.

So I saw a gap. Industry labs had systems people, but they were building for their own internal workloads and their work was often not open. Academic labs had lots of people doing models, and almost nobody doing systems. And systems work has this nice property that if you do it well, it compounds. If you make PyTorch, or later vLLM, a bit faster or more usable, thousands of researchers benefit, including the ones doing the algorithmic work I had become skeptical about.

There was also a very practical consideration. Systems work has a clear notion of being right. Either it runs faster or it does not. Either it is correct or it is not. Coming from a field where a lot of claims were hard to reproduce, that was really attractive. I wanted to work on things where I could actually point to the impact, where I could open GitHub and see people using what I built.

And the last thing I would say is that at the time, large models were just taking off. It became obvious that the frontier was going to be set by who could train and serve these models efficiently, not just by who had the cleverest loss function. So the systems direction felt both intellectually interesting and like it was going to matter a lot. For an academic lab, where you do not have the compute of a big company, being good at systems is also a way to do more with less. That was very appealing.

r001.rationale: The response says academic systems work can benefit thousands of researchers and help a lab do more with less, but it does not clearly say that research conducted at academic-lab scale can be extended to large-scale settings.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me was that machine learning creates new systems problems all the time. Models change, hardware changes, and the way people use them changes. That gives an academic lab opportunities to question assumptions and explore approaches that aren’t yet part of a mature software stack.

You also don’t necessarily need the resources to train the largest model to make a useful contribution. You can identify a bottleneck in how models are trained or served, understand why it happens, and design a better solution. So I saw it as a direction where a small team could do rigorous research with practical impact.

r001.rationale: The response says a small academic team can study training or serving bottlenecks and make practical contributions, but it does not communicate that this research can extend to large-scale settings.

sol-6.1.text:
What attracted me was the gap between a machine-learning model working in a paper and actually running efficiently in practice. A better model doesn’t automatically mean a better system. You have to think about memory, computation, communication, and how all those pieces fit together.

For an academic lab, that creates interesting opportunities. We might not have the resources to train the largest model, but we can study why existing workloads are inefficient and find better ways to run them. A good systems idea can make the same hardware more useful, and it can benefit many different models. That combination of research questions and practical impact made the direction appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response says an academic lab can study inefficiencies and develop ideas that help many models, but it does not clearly state that this research can extend to large-scale settings.
